01: SHOT 01 — Cleopatra stands alone at a high palace window in Alexandria at dawn, seen three-quarters from behind and slightly below, her draped linen catching the first light. Beyond her the harbour opens out: the great lighthouse of Pharos rising pale against a wide gold sky, fishing boats already moving on flat water, the long curve of the royal quarter's colonnades. In the middle ground two palace servants carry folded cloth along a terrace, unaware of her. The mood is quiet and enormous, a young woman looking out over a city she is about to lose.
02: SHOT 02 — A wide establishing view of Alexandria in 48 BC seen from above the rooftops in flat late-morning light. Straight paved avenues run between whitewashed buildings toward the sea; the lighthouse stands at the harbour mouth with ships at anchor around it. In the middle ground a busy market street: awnings, stacked pottery, sacks of grain, a man leading a donkey, two women talking beside a fountain. Egyptian temple pylons stand among Greek colonnades, the two architectures side by side. No figure is the focus; the city itself is the subject.
03: SHOT 03 — Inside a Ptolemaic throne room, Cleopatra stands to one side while her younger brother Ptolemy, a boy of about thirteen in royal Egyptian dress, sits on the throne surrounded by adult advisers in Greek robes. The advisers lean toward the boy, one speaking into his ear, another gesturing dismissively toward Cleopatra without looking at her. Painted columns and a polished stone floor recede behind them. Cleopatra's face is composed and watchful. The composition puts the boy at the centre and her at the edge, which is the entire point of the image.
04: SHOT 04 — Cleopatra on a dusty road outside the city at hard midday, walking away from Alexandria with a small group of loyal attendants and two laden pack animals. The road runs through dry scrub toward flat open country; the city and its lighthouse are small and pale on the horizon behind her. She looks back over her shoulder once. In the middle ground a broken milestone and a stunted tree. Dust hangs in the hot air. The scale is deliberately lonely: a queen reduced to a traveller on a road.
05: SHOT 05 — A Roman war fleet arriving at Alexandria harbour, seen from the quayside at a low angle so the ships loom. Legionaries in segmented armour line the rails; a gangway is being run out; officers stand at the bow. On the stone quay, Egyptian dockworkers and onlookers draw back in a nervous crowd, one man shielding a child. The lighthouse rises behind the masts. Heavy overcast light, the sea grey and choppy. Caesar himself is not visible; this image is about the arrival of Roman power, not the man.
06: SHOT 06 — Cleopatra seated in a plain room by lamplight at a wooden table, in exile, thinking hard. A rolled map or chart is open in front of her, one hand resting flat on it, the other at her chin. Behind her a single narrow window shows deep blue night. In the middle ground an oil lamp, a cup, and a folded travelling cloak over a stool. An older female attendant waits silently in the shadow near the doorway. The image should feel like a plan forming, not like grief.
07: SHOT 07 — A night scene on a small boat crossing dark water toward the lit shore of Alexandria, seen from just above the waterline. Two men row; Cleopatra sits low and wrapped in a dark travelling cloak with her face turned toward the shore. The palace quarter glows with scattered lamps ahead, and Roman sentry fires burn at intervals along the waterfront. Reflections break on the black water. The framing is tight and tense, a small vessel in a lot of darkness, the danger implied by how carefully everyone is sitting still.
08: SHOT 08 — Close on a length of plain bedding cloth being folded and bound with cord on a stone floor by lamplight, hands working quickly in the foreground. The scale is intimate and slightly strange: we see the sack taking shape and understand what it is for before anyone is shown inside it. In the middle ground a servant's sandalled feet and the lower edge of a doorway curtain. Shadows are long and low from a single lamp. No faces; the image is about the object and the quiet urgency around it.
09: SHOT 09 — A servant carries a long bound bundle of bedding over his shoulder through a torchlit palace corridor, walking steadily past two Roman guards who barely glance at him. The corridor recedes in painted columns and patterned floor tiles. The guards stand at ease, one mid-yawn, spears resting. The bundle is unremarkable and that is the tension: the viewer knows, and the guards do not. Warm torchlight on stone, deep shadow between the columns, the carrier's face set and ordinary.
10: SHOT 10 — Inside a Roman officer's quarters converted from a palace room, the bound bundle has just been set down on the floor and the servant is withdrawing. Caesar sits at a writing table across the room, looking up from a document with the beginning of a frown, stylus still in hand. Between them, the bundle's cord is loose and the cloth has begun to shift. Maps and wax tablets are spread on the table; a lamp burns low. The moment is caught exactly one second before anything is explained.
11: SHOT 11 — Cleopatra rising to her feet from the opened bedding cloth in the centre of the room, straightening her dress with complete composure, chin level. Caesar has stood up behind his table, one hand flat on the wood, entirely still. Two Roman officers near the door have frozen mid-step, one with a hand half-raised toward his sword and going no further. The lamplight is warm and low. She is the smallest figure in the room and unmistakably the centre of it.
12: SHOT 12 — Cleopatra and Caesar in conversation across the writing table, both seated now, leaning slightly toward one another. She is speaking and gesturing economically at a map between them; he is listening with his head tilted, unconvinced but interested. A wine cup and a stack of wax tablets sit to one side. Behind them a window shows the harbour at night. This is a negotiation, not a romance: the body language is two people calculating, and the map is the thing they are both looking at.
13: SHOT 13 — Caesar's hand pressing a signet ring into hot wax on a document, seen in tight close-up from above. The wax is bright against the pale papyrus. The edge of a toga sleeve with its purple border enters the frame, and beyond the document the blurred shapes of the table's lamp and cups. A decision made, rendered as a small physical act. The image is deliberately quiet and close after the drama of the previous moment.
14: SHOT 14 — Street fighting in Alexandria: Egyptian soldiers loyal to Ptolemy pressing against a Roman shield line in a narrow paved avenue, seen from a raised angle. The Romans hold a tight formation with overlapping shields; the Egyptians push forward with spears and wicker shields. Dust and smoke drift between the buildings, and a market awning has collapsed across the street. In the far background the lighthouse is just visible through haze. Chaotic middle ground, disciplined foreground line, no single hero figure.
15: SHOT 15 — The bank of the Nile at grey dawn, reeds in the foreground, the wide brown river flowing past. Egyptian soldiers stand at the water's edge looking out at something in the current that we do not see clearly — a dark shape among reeds, deliberately ambiguous and not gruesome. One man has waded in to his knees and stopped. Herons lift off further downstream. The image is sombre and still, the violence entirely off-frame and implied by the men's posture.
16: SHOT 16 — Cleopatra restored, standing in the Alexandrian throne room in full Ptolemaic royal dress, receiving the formal bows of court officials and priests who line both sides of the hall. Sunlight falls in hard shafts from high windows across the polished floor. In the middle ground a scribe records the moment on a papyrus roll; an attendant carries a ceremonial fan. Her expression is controlled rather than triumphant. The composition is symmetrical and formal, the opposite of the crooked, off-centre framing of her earlier scene in this room.
17: SHOT 17 — The steps of a Roman public building at midday, moments after violence: a crowd of togaed senators scattering down the stairs in alarm, some looking back, one dropping a scroll that unrolls across the stone. At the top of the steps a tight knot of figures obscures whatever has happened, seen only as backs and raised arms. Roman columns and statues rise behind them against a hard blue sky. Nothing graphic is shown; the horror is entirely in the direction everyone is running.
18: SHOT 18 — Mark Antony arriving in the east: a Roman general in his forties, powerfully built, with thick dark curling hair and a strong jaw, clearly a different man from Caesar in every respect, standing at the prow of a ship approaching a harbour with a bodyguard behind him. He wears a military cloak over a decorated cuirass and stands with one boot on the rail, expansive and confident. Gulls, rigging, and the shoreline of a Greek-Egyptian port in warm afternoon light. Deliberately physical and swaggering where Caesar was spare and cold.
19: SHOT 19 — A domestic interior in the Alexandrian palace: Cleopatra and Antony seated together on a low couch in soft evening light, three young children of different ages playing on a patterned floor rug nearby, a nurse just visible at the edge of the frame. A bowl of figs and a lamp sit on a low table. The room is rich but lived-in, with a child's wooden toy left on the floor. Calm and warm, the only moment of ordinary domestic life in the whole sequence.
20: SHOT 20 — A council of war in a lamplit hall: Antony standing over a large map table with Egyptian and Roman officers around it, Cleopatra beside him pointing at a coastline. Model ships or markers are set out on the map. The officers' postures are divided — two lean in agreeing, one stands back with folded arms and a closed expression. Heavy shadows, armour catching the lamplight. The disagreement in the room is the subject, and it is written entirely in how the men are standing.
21: SHOT 21 — A naval defeat at sea seen from a distance in flat grey light: a line of warships broken and scattering, two vessels burning with black smoke bending low across the water, others rowing hard away toward the horizon. Wreckage and oars float in the foreground swell. No faces, no deck detail — the ships are small against a very large sea and a heavy sky. The image should read as a formation that has stopped being a formation.
22: SHOT 22 — A dim palace chamber in the aftermath, shutters half closed, hard bars of daylight falling across an empty floor. A Roman military cloak lies discarded over a stool, a cup overturned beside it, a sword sheathed and set against the wall. No people at all. Dust hangs in the light. The room has the specific stillness of somewhere a great deal has just happened and everyone has gone. Restrained, quiet, and final.
23: SHOT 23 — The Alexandrian palace seen from outside at dusk, tall and shuttered, with a Roman standard now planted at its gate and two legionaries posted at the doors. The windows are dark. In the foreground, low and small, an Egyptian street sweeper works past without looking up, and a stray dog crosses the paving. The lighthouse burns out at the harbour mouth as it always has. Three hundred years of a dynasty ending as a change of guard at a door.
24: SHOT 24 — A single lit phone-sized rectangle of warm light held upright in the dark, with the suggestion of an illustrated historical scene glowing inside it, held in a pair of ordinary hands in the lower foreground. Around and behind it the darkness is soft and total. No text, no interface, no lettering of any kind — only the shape of a small bright window into a picture. Calm, modern, and completely separate in mood from everything before it.
25: SHOT 25 — A quiet closing image: many small warm-lit rectangles of light arranged across a dark field at different depths and angles, like windows seen at night, each one glowing faintly with the colours of a different illustrated historical scene. They recede into darkness in every direction. No text, no lettering, no interface. The effect should be of a great many stories held in one place, seen from a distance, and the image should feel like an ending rather than an argument.
